title: Our Publications
text: Our Publications All Working Papers Policy Papers AI Innovation Employment France Europe Democracy Policy Paper · October 2026 Innovation and catch-up in the AI model market Paul Delbouve LIFT Policy Paper 2026-04 — October 2026 AI Innovation Competition In AI, the best model sold for 0.1 dollar per million tokens or less, at least fifty times cheaper than a frontier model, catches up with its quality in less than a year. This catch-up could discourage growing investment, on the order of 715 billion dollars in 2026 for the main AI developers, by reducing the rent that a technological lead provides. On OpenRouter, frontier labs handle only 28% of tokens in August 2026, compared with three quarters in spring 2025, but still collect 71% of revenue thanks to higher prices. Relative to its competitors, a provider that releases a frontier model sees its imputed revenue roughly double in the following months, and the users of a model facing new competition mostly switch to other high-end models. This equilibrium rests on exceptional growth in consumption and remains fragile: frontier labs’ share of revenue fell from 82% to 71% between mid-July and mid-August 2026. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Policy Paper · October 2026 Rising AI spending and the rise of open-weight models Antonin Bergeaud , Paul Delbouve , Etienne Grass LIFT Policy Paper 2026-03 — October 2026 AI France Open models Firms’ AI spending is rising even as the unit cost of a token falls sharply: the increase comes from volumes far more than from prices. On OpenRouter, the share of open-weight models rises from 40% to 73% of tokens between January and August 2026, and from 11% to 34% of spending. Users attributed to France devote 31.0% of their spending to open models, compared with 19.3% worldwide. Calls to open models are four times longer than in January, but their average cost is only 3.8 times higher: the cost advantage persists. Reallocation toward open models accounts for 43% of the simulated decline in the cost of a constant French basket; it opens room for wider deployment rather than an automatic saving, which invites organizations to reason in terms of cost per completed task. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Policy Paper · October 2026 Generative AI: a freeze on youth hiring in exposed occupations Antonin Bergeaud , Antoine Bertheau, Simon Bunel , Oscar Degos , Marco Guido Palladino LIFT Policy Paper 2026-02 — October 2026 AI France Employment Labor market Since November 2022, hires of 21-29-year-olds on open-ended contracts have fallen by 28.3% in the occupations most exposed to generative AI, compared with 7.5% in the least exposed. Separations are also falling, but less than hires: worker turnover is slowing and the market is freezing for young people in exposed occupations. The gap narrows with age, from more than 20 percentage points among 21-29-year-olds to less than 4 points after age 50, and it persists when fixed-term contracts are added to open-ended ones. It is not driven by developers alone, whose hires of young people on open-ended contracts fall by 42%: without them, the gap remains 17 points. Firms that report intensive use of AI hire relatively fewer young people, while their total headcount does not clearly diverge from that of other firms. The analysis covers labor turnover data from January 2019 to March 2026, matched with the Banque de France business survey, with which this work was carried out. The method and the full set of results are detailed in LIFT Working Paper 2026-02. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Working Paper · October 2026 Occupational exposure to generative AI, firm adoption and labor market dynamics in France Marco Guido Palladino , Antonin Bergeaud , Antoine Bertheau, Simon Bunel , Oscar Degos LIFT Working Paper 2026-02 — October 2026 AI France Employment Labor market This paper studies how employment in France evolves with occupations’ exposure to generative artificial intelligence and with workers’ age. We build a new index that ranks occupations from least to most exposed, then draw on comprehensive administrative data on hires and separations between January 2019 and March 2026. Since November 2022, the month of ChatGPT’s public launch, both hires and separations on open-ended contracts have fallen more in the most exposed occupations, especially among young people. These trends point to a kind of freeze in labor turnover for new entrants in exposed occupations, with fewer entries and fewer exits. The result also holds among firms that report intensive use of AI: their hiring of young people on open-ended contracts declines relative to other firms, with no clear divergence in the evolution of their total employment compared with other firms. The main results are presented in short form in LIFT Policy Paper 2026-02. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Policy Paper · September 2026 Why AI is not (yet) making France more productive Antonin Bergeaud , Simon Bunel LIFT Policy Paper 2026-01 — September 2026 AI France Productivity France spends as much as the United States on information technology (6.5% of GDP in 2025, compared with 6.8%), but its hourly productivity has stagnated since 2015: its lag stems from the return on this spending. Upstream, it is at the European average for research, patents and capital, but its computing power per capita is more than 50% below the European average. The French use generative AI individually at least as much as other Europeans, but their firms integrate it less: only 18% use it, compared with 26% in Germany, and integration remains shallow, concentrated in product development rather than in cross-cutting functions. This lag is above all organizational: 69% of French workers receive neither encouragement, nor tools, nor training in AI from their employer, compared with 44% in the United States. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Working Paper · February 2026 Politics at work: workplace experience and political divides among employees in France Yann Algan , Antonin Bergeaud , Camille Frouard LIFT Working Paper 2026-01 — February 2026 (first released as an HEC Policy Note) Democracy Work France Politics Drawing on a survey of 3,900 private-sector employees in 2024-2025, this note analyzes how everyday experience at work shapes political divides in France. The axis that separates electorates at work is neither wages nor socio-occupational category, but the quality of the social ties experienced day to day in the firm. Employees close to the Rassemblement National (RN) show strong trust in their firm but distrust their colleagues and are socially isolated, while employees close to La France insoumise (LFI) distrust management but trust their colleagues. One third of employees, the most isolated at work, are unaffiliated and do not vote: disengagement at work precedes civic disengagement. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Working Paper · October 2025 Cost of Failure, Disruptive Innovation and Targeted Flexicurity Yann Coatanlem, Oliver Coste LIFT Working Paper 2025-03 — October 2025 Innovation Europe Labor market This paper expands earlier work by assembling a larger sample of restructuring plans (250 plans) to measure the restructuring costs borne by large firms and to assess their links with business R&D in disruptive sectors (tech/biotech). The authors confirm a wide transatlantic gap, with Germany at 31 months of average salary versus 7 months in the United States, and identify low-cost outliers within Europe (Denmark, Switzerland). They show a strong negative correlation between restructuring costs and R&D intensity in tech and biotech, and conclude with recommendations for targeted reforms of employment protection laws that preserve social protection while restoring the agility critical for disruptive innovation. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF ↓ Working Paper · July 2025 Artificial intelligence in the service of innovation: an analysis of patent data Antonin Bergeaud LIFT Working Paper 2025-02 — July 2025 AI Innovation The impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies on economic growth depends largely on their ability to increase research productivity. In this article, we propose an original measure of the diffusion of AI across technologies, based on patents filed in the United States since 1990. Our methodology identifies patents that incorporate AI through their references to academic publications classified as AI. As of December 2024, about 5% of patents filed can thus be characterized as using AI. This approach captures the integration of AI into other technological fields, consistent with its nature as a general-purpose technology. We show that these “AI” patents systematically display higher quality indicators than other patents, according to several standard metrics. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Working Paper · July 2025 The diffusion of artificial intelligence in France Philippe Aghion , Antonin Bergeaud , Simon Bunel , Paul Delbouve LIFT Working Paper 2025-01 — July 2025 AI France Tracker Employment Using more than 120 million job postings published online in France since 2019, this study examines the characteristics of the diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) in firms and its effects on employment. AI diffusion turns out to be highly heterogeneous: it is particularly advanced in certain sectors (IT, finance, consulting) and within large pioneering firms. We show that the firms most exposed to AI were significantly more inclined to hire AI specialists as soon as ChatGPT appeared. At the same time, we observe a relative decline in job creation in the occupations most exposed to AI, but an increase in labor productivity in the firms concerned. Abstract ↓ Read → PDF in French ↓ Working Paper · January 2024 Exposure to generative artificial intelligence and employment: an application to the French socio-occupational classification Antonin Bergeaud LIFT Working Paper 2024-01 — January 2024 AI France Employment This paper analyzes the exposure of French occupations to generative artificial intelligence through the socio-occupational classification. Drawing on O*NET data and a GPT-4 assessment protocol, it proposes two indices: substitutability and complementarity. The results reveal strong heterogeneity across occupations, with higher exposure for the most skilled occupations. This approach helps to better identify automation risks and complementarity opportunities, and underscores the need to account for adoption costs and endogenous transformations to anticipate impacts on employment. title: Team
text: Team Members Researchers, economists and experts of the Laboratory of Innovation and Future Transformations. Core members Co-director Antonin Bergeaud Associate professor at HEC Paris, research affiliate of the CEP/LSE, the CEPR and the Collège de France’s Innovation Lab. His research focuses on growth, productivity and innovation. Co-director Yann Algan Associate Dean of Pre-Experience Programs and professor of economics at HEC Paris. His research focuses on trust, well-being in organizations and the evaluation of public policy. Core member Clément Mazet-Sonilhac Assistant professor at Bocconi University, he will join HEC Paris on January 1, 2027. His research focuses on technological change and financial intermediation. Fellows Fellow Simon Bunel Administrator of INSEE, postdoctoral researcher at the INSEAD Stone Centre and adjunct professor at the ENS. His work focuses on the macroeconomic effects of AI. Fellow Flavio Calvino Senior economist at the OECD. His research analyzes the impact of digital technologies and AI on firm dynamics and productivity. Fellow Marco G. Palladino Senior economist at the Banque de France and adjunct professor at Sciences Po. His research focuses on the role of firms in wage setting and on the effects of AI on the labor market. Associate researchers Associate researcher Thomas Renault Professor of economics at Université Paris-Saclay. His research lies at the intersection of economics, finance and technology, using machine learning and semantic analysis tools. Associate researcher Éric Hazan Entrepreneur, investor and lecturer at HEC Paris and Sciences Po. His work explores how AI is transforming firms, work and European competitiveness. Associate researcher Pascal Saint-Amans Former director of the OECD Centre for Tax Policy and Administration. He teaches at HEC Paris and the University of Lausanne. Associate researcher Arnaud Dyèvre Assistant professor of economics at HEC Paris. His research focuses on growth, innovation and the role of public research in the diffusion of knowledge. PhD students PhD student Paul Delbouve PhD student in macroeconomics at PSE (EHESS) and researcher at the French Ministry of the Economy and Finance. He studies the diffusion of AI in the French economy. PhD student Gabriela Terra Research staff Research assistant Valentin Auplat de Lustrac Research assistant Nil Baruchel Research assistant Oscar Degos Research assistant Rémy Siahaan-Gensollen Research assistant Mathieu Valibhay Research assistant Arthur Felix Research assistant Luca Milani Research assistant Pierre Clarke Research assistant Carla Abon Scientific council Scientific council Philippe Aghion Professor at the Collège de France, INSEAD and the London School of Economics, 2025 Nobel Prize in Economics for his work on innovation and growth. Scientific council Christophe Pérignon Professor of finance and Associate Dean for Research at HEC Paris. His research focuses on artificial intelligence in finance.

Innovation data Productivity International productivity GDP per capita, hourly labor productivity and TFP (1890–2024) Indicator: Log scale CSV Reset Countries: Source: Long Term Productivity Database (A. Bergeaud, G. Cette, R. Lecat), version 2.7 (February 2026). GDP per capita and productivity in international dollars at 2020 PPP. About this tracker This dashboard shows the evolution of three key indicators of economic performance since 1890 for 24 economies (23 countries + the euro area): GDP per capita : average standard of living (in 2020 PPP $) Hourly labor productivity : value added per hour worked (2020 PPP $ per hour) Total factor productivity (TFP) : combined efficiency of labor and capital The second chart shows the growth waves : the growth rate filtered with a Hodrick-Prescott filter (λ=500), which isolates the long-run trend of the series. Authors This tracker is based on the Long Term Productivity Database developed by: Antonin Bergeaud Gilbert Cette Rémy Lecat Methodology The data come from the Long Term Productivity Database (Bergeaud, Cette & Lecat), which compiles and harmonizes multiple sources: GDP per capita : Maddison Project Database, national accounts Hourly labor productivity : hours worked from national and international sources (OECD, ILO) TFP : computed from a Cobb-Douglas production function with time-varying factor shares Waves : growth rate smoothed with a Hodrick-Prescott filter (λ=500) to isolate the long-run trend The series cover 24 economies from 1890 to 2024. Methodological breaks between sources are corrected by splicing to ensure the continuity of the series. Reference Bergeaud, A., Cette, G. & Lecat, R. (2016). “Productivity Trends in Advanced Countries between 1890 and 2012” . Review of Income and Wealth , 62(3), 420-444. Update Data as of October 1, 2026: version 2.7 of the Long Term Productivity Database (February 2026). The tracker is updated with each new version of the database. With version 2.7, levels are expressed in 2020 PPP dollars (instead of 2017 PPP previously) and the series have been revised; recent levels are markedly higher than with version 2.6.

About this tracker This dashboard tracks inventive activity in high-technology sectors through international patent filings (PCT). It measures the contribution of each country and region to key technologies (AI, biotechnology, information technology, green technologies and semiconductors) since the 1980s. Author This tracker is developed by Antonin Bergeaud — HEC Paris, LSE, CEPR. Methodology Source data The patents analyzed are international applications filed under the Patent Cooperation Treaty (PCT) of the World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO). The data are extracted from Google Patents Public Data via BigQuery. The PCT covers filings in more than 150 member countries and is a reliable indicator of international inventive activity. Fractional counting Each patent is attributed to its inventors’ countries fractionally using the OECD RegPat database. If a patent has 3 inventors (2 in France, 1 in Germany), France receives 2/3 of the patent and Germany 1/3. This method avoids double counting and reflects each country’s actual contribution. title: Breakthrough innovation
text: Breakthrough innovation Breakthrough patents by European country Innovation Patents Breakthrough patents by European country and technology field. Patent abstracts -- European countries -- NUTS2 regions -- Period covered -- Indicator: Novelty Breakthrough CSV Reset Trend over time Countries: Novelty by technology field CSV Comparison by country CSV Indicator: Novelty Breakthrough Period: All years Top 10 European regions CSV Indicator: Novelty Breakthrough Period: All years Map of Europe Sources: 4.6 million abstracts of EPO patents filed from 1983 to 2024 (Google Patents). Inventor location via REGPAT (OECD, August 2026 edition). CPC classification (4 fields). Population: World Bank. Scores computed by cosine similarity on embeddings of the English abstracts ( PatentSBERTa_V2 ). Methodology inspired by Kelly, Papanikolaou, Seru & Taddy (2021, AER Insights) . 2024 incomplete: patent applications are published about 18 months after filing, and the year still contains only about 83% of the patents of a complete year. Shares are little affected; the 2024 figures per million inhabitants will be revised upward. About this tracker This dashboard analyzes 4.6 million patents filed with the European Patent Office (EPO) between 1983 and 2024 , covering 24 European countries. It identifies breakthrough patents and measures their output by country, by region (NUTS2) and by technology field. A patent is considered a breakthrough patent if it is in the top 1% of the annual distribution according to one of the following two measures: Novelty ( backward-looking ): measures how different a patent is from prior art at the time of filing. Formally, it is the sum of the cosine similarities between the embedding vector of the abstract and those of all patents filed in the previous 5 years. A patent is classified as highly novel if it has a low score (bottom 1%), indicating that it is distant from existing technologies. This measure is available for all years, including the most recent. Breakthrough : ratio between future influence and proximity to prior art (forward_sum / backward_sum). A patent is classified as a breakthrough patent if it has a high ratio (top 1%), which identifies patents that are both very different from existing technologies and very influential on future innovations. Note: this measure is not available after 2019 because it requires observing the patents filed in the following 5 years. The country charts show the number of breakthrough patents per million inhabitants . Authors This tracker is developed by: Antonin Bergeaud Dario Marino Methodology Computing the scores (KPST) The methodology is inspired by Kelly, Papanikolaou, Seru and Taddy (2021, AER Insights) : Text embeddings : the English abstract of each patent is turned into a high-dimensional numerical vector with the PatentSBERTa_V2 model, a Sentence-BERT model pre-trained on patent texts. When a patent has an abstract only in German or French (about 16% of patents), the machine English translation from Google Patents is used: all patents are thus compared in the same language. Novelty score ( backward_sum ): sum of the cosine similarities between the vector of the patent’s abstract and those of all patents filed in the previous 5 years. A low score means that the patent is far from the state of the art. Future proximity ( forward_sum ): sum of the cosine similarities between the vector of the abstract and those of all patents filed in the following 5 years. Used as the numerator of the breakthrough score. Breakthrough score ( importance ): ratio forward_sum / backward_sum . A high ratio identifies patents that are both far from existing technologies and close to future innovations. Definition of breakthrough patents A patent is classified in the top 1% within each filing year: Highly novel : bottom 1% of the distribution of backward_sum (the most distant from prior art) Breakthrough : top 1% of the distribution of importance (the highest forward/backward ratio) Thresholds are computed separately for each year to control for changes in the distributions over time. Novelty index by technology field The index shown in the chart by technology field measures the relative gap between the average novelty score of a technology field and the overall average: \[\text{Index} = \frac{\overline{backward\_sum}_{\text{global}} - \overline{backward\_sum}_{\text{field}}}{\overline{backward\_sum}_{\text{global}}}\] A positive index means that the field’s patents are on average more novel than the average. The index is computed each year. Technology classification (CPC) The chart of novelty by technology field uses 4 fields of the Cooperative Patent Classification (CPC, the harmonized EPO/USPTO system): CPC code Field G06N AI / Machine learning C12N Biotechnology A61K Pharmaceuticals H01L and H10 Semiconductors (H10 takes over H01L since the CPC reforms; current codes apply to all years) Geographic attribution By country: patents are attributed based on the location of the inventors (source: REGPAT, OECD). When a patent has several inventors from different countries, it is counted fractionally (1/N per inventor). By region (NUTS2): patents are attributed to NUTS2 regions according to the regional code of the inventor’s residence. The regional data cover about 380 European NUTS2 regions. Data sources Patents : abstracts and CPC codes of EPO publications, Google Patents Public Data (BigQuery) — 4,649,815 EPO patents filed from 1983 to 2024 Location : REGPAT (OECD, August 2026 edition) — country and region (NUTS2) of origin of the inventors Classification : CPC codes (Cooperative Patent Classification) — 4 targeted fields Population : World Bank (indicator SP.POP.TOTL) — for normalization per million inhabitants Update Data as of October 6, 2026: EPO publications up to September 16, 2026 (Google Patents) and REGPAT (OECD) of August 2026. The tracker is updated after each new REGPAT edition. 2024 is incomplete: patent applications are published about 18 months after filing, and the year still contains only about 83% of the patents of a complete year. Shares are little affected; the 2024 figures per million inhabitants will be revised upward.

title: Innovation and catch-up in the AI model market
text: Innovation and catch-up in the AI model market LIFT Policy Paper 2026-04 — October 2026 AI Innovation Competition Published October 2026 Abstract In AI, the best model sold for 0.1 dollar per million tokens or less, at least fifty times cheaper than a frontier model, catches up with its quality in less than a year. This catch-up could discourage growing investment, on the order of 715 billion dollars in 2026 for the main AI developers, by reducing the rent that a technological lead provides. On OpenRouter, frontier labs handle only 28% of tokens in August 2026, compared with three quarters in spring 2025, but still collect 71% of revenue thanks to higher prices. Relative to its competitors, a provider that releases a frontier model sees its imputed revenue roughly double in the following months, and the users of a model facing new competition mostly switch to other high-end models. This equilibrium rests on exceptional growth in consumption and remains fragile: frontier labs’ share of revenue fell from 82% to 71% between mid-July and mid-August 2026. title: Rising AI spending and the rise of open-weight models
text: Rising AI spending and the rise of open-weight models LIFT Policy Paper 2026-03 — October 2026 AI France Open models Published October 2026 Abstract Firms’ AI spending is rising even as the unit cost of a token falls sharply: the increase comes from volumes far more than from prices. On OpenRouter, the share of open-weight models rises from 40% to 73% of tokens between January and August 2026, and from 11% to 34% of spending. Users attributed to France devote 31.0% of their spending to open models, compared with 19.3% worldwide. Calls to open models are four times longer than in January, but their average cost is only 3.8 times higher: the cost advantage persists. Reallocation toward open models accounts for 43% of the simulated decline in the cost of a constant French basket; it opens room for wider deployment rather than an automatic saving, which invites organizations to reason in terms of cost per completed task. title: Generative AI: a freeze on youth hiring in exposed occupations
text: Generative AI: a freeze on youth hiring in exposed occupations LIFT Policy Paper 2026-02 — October 2026 AI France Employment Labor market Published October 2026 Abstract Since November 2022, hires of 21-29-year-olds on open-ended contracts have fallen by 28.3% in the occupations most exposed to generative AI, compared with 7.5% in the least exposed. Separations are also falling, but less than hires: worker turnover is slowing and the market is freezing for young people in exposed occupations. The gap narrows with age, from more than 20 percentage points among 21-29-year-olds to less than 4 points after age 50, and it persists when fixed-term contracts are added to open-ended ones. It is not driven by developers alone, whose hires of young people on open-ended contracts fall by 42%: without them, the gap remains 17 points. Firms that report intensive use of AI hire relatively fewer young people, while their total headcount does not clearly diverge from that of other firms. The analysis covers labor turnover data from January 2019 to March 2026, matched with the Banque de France business survey, with which this work was carried out. The method and the full set of results are detailed in LIFT Working Paper 2026-02. title: Occupational exposure to generative AI, firm adoption and labor market dynamics in France
text: Occupational exposure to generative AI, firm adoption and labor market dynamics in France LIFT Working Paper 2026-02 — October 2026 AI France Employment Labor market Published October 2026 Abstract This paper studies how employment in France evolves with occupations’ exposure to generative artificial intelligence and with workers’ age. We build a new index that ranks occupations from least to most exposed, then draw on comprehensive administrative data on hires and separations between January 2019 and March 2026. Since November 2022, the month of ChatGPT’s public launch, both hires and separations on open-ended contracts have fallen more in the most exposed occupations, especially among young people. These trends point to a kind of freeze in labor turnover for new entrants in exposed occupations, with fewer entries and fewer exits. The result also holds among firms that report intensive use of AI: their hiring of young people on open-ended contracts declines relative to other firms, with no clear divergence in the evolution of their total employment compared with other firms. The main results are presented in short form in LIFT Policy Paper 2026-02. title: Why AI is not (yet) making France more productive
text: Why AI is not (yet) making France more productive LIFT Policy Paper 2026-01 — September 2026 AI France Productivity Published September 2026 Abstract France spends as much as the United States on information technology (6.5% of GDP in 2025, compared with 6.8%), but its hourly productivity has stagnated since 2015: its lag stems from the return on this spending. Upstream, it is at the European average for research, patents and capital, but its computing power per capita is more than 50% below the European average. The French use generative AI individually at least as much as other Europeans, but their firms integrate it less: only 18% use it, compared with 26% in Germany, and integration remains shallow, concentrated in product development rather than in cross-cutting functions. This lag is above all organizational: 69% of French workers receive neither encouragement, nor tools, nor training in AI from their employer, compared with 44% in the United States. title: Politics at work: workplace experience and political divides among employees in France
text: Politics at work: workplace experience and political divides among employees in France LIFT Working Paper 2026-01 — February 2026 (first released as an HEC Policy Note) Democracy Work France Politics Published February 1, 2026 Abstract Drawing on a survey of 3,900 private-sector employees in 2024-2025, this note analyzes how everyday experience at work shapes political divides in France. The axis that separates electorates at work is neither wages nor socio-occupational category, but the quality of the social ties experienced day to day in the firm. Employees close to the Rassemblement National (RN) show strong trust in their firm but distrust their colleagues and are socially isolated, while employees close to La France insoumise (LFI) distrust management but trust their colleagues. One third of employees, the most isolated at work, are unaffiliated and do not vote: disengagement at work precedes civic disengagement. title: Cost of Failure, Disruptive Innovation and Targeted Flexicurity
text: Cost of Failure, Disruptive Innovation and Targeted Flexicurity LIFT Working Paper 2025-03 — October 2025 Innovation Europe Labor market Published October 1, 2025 Abstract This paper expands earlier work by assembling a larger sample of restructuring plans (250 plans) to measure the restructuring costs borne by large firms and to assess their links with business R&D in disruptive sectors (tech/biotech). The authors confirm a wide transatlantic gap, with Germany at 31 months of average salary versus 7 months in the United States, and identify low-cost outliers within Europe (Denmark, Switzerland). They show a strong negative correlation between restructuring costs and R&D intensity in tech and biotech, and conclude with recommendations for targeted reforms of employment protection laws that preserve social protection while restoring the agility critical for disruptive innovation. title: Artificial intelligence in the service of innovation: an analysis of patent data
text: Artificial intelligence in the service of innovation: an analysis of patent data LIFT Working Paper 2025-02 — July 2025 AI Innovation Published July 20, 2025 Abstract The impact of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies on economic growth depends largely on their ability to increase research productivity. In this article, we propose an original measure of the diffusion of AI across technologies, based on patents filed in the United States since 1990. Our methodology identifies patents that incorporate AI through their references to academic publications classified as AI. As of December 2024, about 5% of patents filed can thus be characterized as using AI. This approach captures the integration of AI into other technological fields, consistent with its nature as a general-purpose technology. We show that these “AI” patents systematically display higher quality indicators than other patents, according to several standard metrics in the literature. title: The diffusion of artificial intelligence in France
text: The diffusion of artificial intelligence in France LIFT Working Paper 2025-01 — July 2025 AI France Tracker Employment Published July 10, 2025 Abstract Using more than 120 million job postings published online in France since 2019, this study examines the characteristics of the diffusion of artificial intelligence (AI) in firms and its effects on employment. AI diffusion turns out to be highly heterogeneous: it is particularly advanced in certain sectors (IT, finance, consulting) and within large pioneering firms. This heterogeneity is also visible geographically, with AI job postings highly concentrated in employment zones that host research clusters or specialized industrial hubs (semiconductors, insurance, aeronautics, etc.). We show that the firms most exposed to AI were significantly more inclined to hire AI specialists as soon as ChatGPT appeared. At the same time, we observe a relative decline in job creation in the occupations most exposed to AI. However, hiring in AI occupations goes hand in hand with an increase in labor productivity and revenue, together with an increase in total employment in the firms concerned, driven by highly exposed occupations at the expense of less exposed ones. title: Exposure to generative artificial intelligence and employment: an application to the French socio-occupational classification
text: Exposure to generative artificial intelligence and employment: an application to the French socio-occupational classification LIFT Working Paper 2024-01 — January 2024 AI France Employment Published January 1, 2024 Abstract This paper analyzes the exposure of French occupations to generative artificial intelligence through the socio-occupational classification. Drawing on O*NET data and a GPT-4 assessment protocol, it proposes two indices: substitutability and complementarity. The results reveal strong heterogeneity across occupations, with higher exposure for the most skilled occupations. This approach helps to better identify automation risks and complementarity opportunities, and underscores the need to account for adoption costs and endogenous transformations to anticipate impacts on employment.
